clue.text: Succeed like producer of Carmen …

definitions.meaning: to succeed is to do well or thrive
the first name of Mérimée, the French author whose novella Carmen inspired Bizet's opera

explanation.surface: Someone is told to do well, just like the creator of the famous Carmen.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrive or flourish is to succeed, and Mérimée, who wrote the novella Carmen, had this first name.

clue.text: Parnassian poet's name not sullied

parts.note: his name other than 'Sully' is his surname, with a play on sullied

explanation.surface: A poet of the Parnassian school keeps an unblemished reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Sully Prudhomme, a leading French Parnassian poet, won the first Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue.text: Sailing, perhaps (as Eliot was at Faber)

definitions.meaning: aboard a ship, as when at sea
T. S. Eliot served as a director of the publisher Faber

explanation.surface: Notes T. S. Eliot's position at his publishing house, with a nautical twist.
explanation.definitionFit: Passengers on a ship are aboard it, and Eliot sat among the directors of Faber.

clue.text: "None of your dam —" (Meredith, One of Our Conquerors)

definitions.text: "None of your dam —" (Meredith, One of Our Conquerors)

parts.words: "None of your dam —" (Meredith, One of Our Conquerors)
parts.note: fill the gap in George Meredith's line with a word meaning a fine point of etiquette

explanation.surface: A quotation from George Meredith with its final word missing.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's speaker scorns fussy, finicking points of formal etiquette.

clue.text: Floated by Heyerdahl! to prove a point

definitions.text: Floated by Heyerdahl! to prove a point

parts.words: Floated by Heyerdahl! to prove a point
parts.note: Thor Heyerdahl crossed the Pacific on Kon-Tiki, a balsa log vessel, to show early peoples could have made the voyage

explanation.surface: Suggests an idea floated by the Norwegian explorer to win an argument.
explanation.definitionFit: Heyerdahl's Kon-Tiki was a simple vessel of lashed balsa logs.

clue.text: … or perversely urge hit from theatre director

indicators.note: doing something perversely means doing it in a contrary, twisted way, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, someone wilfully urges a hit show out of a stage director.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perversely' rearranges URGEHIT. The leading dots and 'or' tie the clue to 1 Across. Sir Tyrone Guthrie was a celebrated British theatre director.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Tyrone Guthrie was a leading twentieth-century stage director, founder of a famous Minneapolis playhouse.

clue.text: Odd as Gogol revised by Heller

indicators.note: a revised text has been reworked, so these letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A peculiar Russian writer is rewritten by the author of Catch-22.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revised' rearranges ODDASGOGOL. Joseph Heller's 1979 novel Good as Gold follows a Jewish academic drawn into Washington politics.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Heller wrote the satirical novel Good as Gold in 1979.

clue.text: Thanks thus expressed by poet

indicators.note: expressed means spoken, so the words are heard rather than read

parts.note: ta is informal British for thanks, and so means thus

explanation.surface: Gratitude voiced this way by a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken, 'ta, so' sounds like the name of Torquato Tasso, the Italian Renaissance poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Torquato Tasso wrote the epic Jerusalem Delivered in sixteenth-century Italy.

clue.text: "Never a man's thought in the world keeps to the -- —better than thine" (Henry IV Part 2)

definitions.text: "Never a man's thought in the world keeps to the -- —better than thine" (Henry IV Part 2)

parts.words: "Never a man's thought in the world keeps to the -- —better than thine" (Henry IV Part 2)
parts.note: fill the gap in Shakespeare's line with a word for the highway

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's Henry IV Part 2 with a gap to fill.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's speaker means nobody's thinking stays more firmly on the beaten track or highway.

clue.text: Stage direction from The Green Terror

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: A theatrical instruction taken from a play called The Green Terror.
explanation.definitionFit: The instruction telling an actor to come on stage is a standard script direction.

clue.text: Not a country boy, this Pope?

definitions.meaning: someone who is not from the countryside belongs to the town or city
several popes took this name, including the one who launched the First Crusade

explanation.surface: Asks whether a city-bred lad might be a particular pontiff.
explanation.definitionFit: City-dwelling is the opposite of rural, and eight popes have reigned under this name.

clue.text: Historian stirs for a change

indicators.note: 'for a change' says the letters before it are made to take a different order

explanation.surface: A historian shakes things up, just to make a difference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' rearranges STIRSFORA. Jean Froissart was the fourteenth-century French chronicler of the Hundred Years' War.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Froissart wrote the Chronicles, the great medieval account of the Hundred Years' War.

clue.text: Hot foxhole for Reade's vicar of Gouda

parts.note: H is the usual abbreviation for hot, as on a tap
a fox's burrow is called its earth

explanation.surface: A warm burrow is offered to a clergyman from a Charles Reade novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Charles Reade's novel The Cloister and the Hearth ends with its hero Gerard as vicar of Gouda, torn between the monastic life and home.
explanation.definitionFit: Reade's Gerard, later vicar of Gouda, is torn between the cloister and the domestic fireside named in the book's title.

clue.text: Surprise, for example, from Patrick O'Brian

definitions.text: Surprise, for example, from Patrick O'Brian

parts.words: Surprise, for example, from Patrick O'Brian
parts.note: HMS Surprise is Jack Aubrey's frigate in Patrick O'Brian's naval novels, an instance of a type of armed sailing ship

explanation.surface: Something unexpected turns up in a Patrick O'Brian novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A frigate such as O'Brian's Surprise is an armed naval vessel of the sailing era.

clue.text: Celtic legends, new edition, gain in boom

indicators.note: a new edition reworks a text, so these letters appear in a fresh arrangement

explanation.surface: A fresh printing of Celtic tales profits from a publishing boom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new edition' rearranges GAININBOOM. The Mabinogion is the medieval Welsh collection of tales.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mabinogion is the medieval Welsh prose collection of myths and tales.

clue.text: An example of Siegfried Lenz

parts.note: an example to copy, and also the English sense of Das Vorbild, a novel by the German writer Siegfried Lenz

explanation.surface: A sample taken from the work of the German novelist Siegfried Lenz.
explanation.definitionFit: An exemplar to imitate is a pattern, and Lenz's novel Das Vorbild takes that sense as its title.

clue.text: Observant as Odysseus' dog

parts.note: Odysseus' faithful hound was named Argus, sharing the name of the hundred-eyed watchman of myth, so watchful eyes like his

explanation.surface: Someone is as watchful as the faithful hound of Homer's hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth gives his name to an idiom for vigilant watchfulness.

clue.text: Tamerlane's city left a mark in the sand

indicators.note: in places one set of letters within another

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: The great conqueror's capital left only a trace in the desert sand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' looks like a direction or a leftover letter L but is only a link word. Tamerlane (Timur) made Samarkand, in modern Uzbekistan, his capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Timur, also called Tamerlane, made this Silk Road city in Uzbekistan the capital of his empire.

clue.text: Surprise success, like Black Beauty?

definitions.meaning: an unexpected winner, a contender whose ability was unknown
Anna Sewell's Black Beauty is a black horse

explanation.surface: Asks whether an unexpected triumph resembles Anna Sewell's famous horse.
explanation.definitionFit: An unexpected winner is an idiomatic sense, while Sewell's black steed is literally a horse of dark colour.

clue.text: Journalistic leader, perhaps

parts.note: seems to mean a chief of a newspaper, but a leader is also the British word for a newspaper's opinion article

explanation.surface: Describes a person at the head of a newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: A leader or leading article is the newspaper column expressing the paper's own opinion.

clue.text: A. S. Byatt found eponymous characters among dissenters?

definitions.text: A. S. Byatt found eponymous characters

parts.note: among means in
dissenting religious groups are sects

explanation.surface: A. S. Byatt discovers her title characters among nonconformists.
explanation.walkthrough: Byatt's novella Morpho Eugenia was filmed as Angels and Insects, the book's title naming creatures among its subjects.
explanation.definitionFit: Byatt's Angels and Insects takes its title in part from the creatures studied by its naturalist hero.

clue.text: Harpagon or any other answer would have to be close

definitions.text: Harpagon or any other answer would have to be close

parts.words: Harpagon or any other answer would have to be close
parts.note: Harpagon is the money-hoarder of Molière's comedy L'Avare, and close means tight-fisted

explanation.surface: Suggests that any rival solution would need to be near the mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Molière's Harpagon is the archetypal hoarder, and a close person is stingy with money.

clue.text: Unexpected treason from legislator: sufficient to upset a Nestor

indicators.note: something unexpected comes out a surprising way, so these letters appear in a new order

explanation.surface: A lawmaker commits treason, which is enough to upset an elderly counsellor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unexpected' rearranges TREASON. The rest of the clue gives the same letters again: 'sufficient to upset a Nestor' says that A NESTOR also rearranges to the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a senate is a lawmaker in an upper chamber.

clue.text: Compendium of humour (black, in Beddoes's case)

definitions.text: Compendium of humour (black, in Beddoes's case)

parts.words: Compendium of humour (black, in Beddoes's case)
parts.note: a collection of jokes; Thomas Lovell Beddoes wrote the macabre verse drama Death's ...

explanation.surface: Describes a collection of comic pieces, with a darker one by a Romantic poet.
explanation.definitionFit: A collection of jokes and witticisms, the kind Beddoes darkened in his drama Death's Jest-Book.

clue.text: Short month that is in Strindberg play

parts.note: Jul is the short form of July
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A brief month features in a play by Strindberg.
explanation.walkthrough: Strindberg's play is Miss Julie (Fröken Julie), named for its title character.
explanation.definitionFit: Strindberg's naturalistic tragedy is called Miss Julie, after its aristocratic heroine.

clue.text: Accent in papal letter

definitions.meaning: a curved diacritic mark indicating a short vowel
a short papal document, less formal than a bull

explanation.surface: A diacritical mark appears in a letter from the Pope.
explanation.definitionFit: A small curved mark shows a short vowel, and a pope's brief letter takes the same Latin-derived name.

clue.text: Forester propsed death to them

parts.note: C. S. Forester wrote the Napoleonic novel Death to the ..., so the people he wished death upon

explanation.surface: A woodsman has suggested killing some group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'propsed' is an OCR slip for 'proposed'. Forester is the novelist C. S. Forester, not a woodsman.
explanation.definitionFit: C. S. Forester's novel Death to the French names Napoleon's soldiers as its target.

clue.text: Man, perhaps, in Primo Levi's Letters

indicators.note: in says the letters sit within the words that follow

explanation.surface: Someone, perhaps, appears in the correspondence of Primo Levi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' is the Isle of Man, an island in the Irish Sea; 'Primo' is part of the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man is an example of an island.

clue.text: Freshly-formed rut is clue to Tennyson's poet-hero

indicators.note: something freshly formed has been made anew, so the following letters take a new shape

explanation.surface: A new groove becomes a hint to identify a poet Tennyson wrote about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Freshly-formed' rearranges RUTISCLUE. Tennyson's dramatic monologue Lucretius has the Roman poet as its speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's monologue takes the Roman author of De Rerum Natura as its central figure.

clue.text: Later than Robert W. Anderson's 1973 novel

definitions.meaning: the title of a 1973 novel by the American playwright Robert Anderson

explanation.surface: Something comes subsequent to a particular 1970s novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Following in time means coming subsequently, and Robert Anderson's 1973 novel bears that one-word title.

clue.text: Great failure of. K. Brunel (English in reverse)

parts.note: a ship going astern is moving backwards

explanation.surface: Notes the engineer Brunel's big flop, with a remark about English going backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of. K.' is an OCR slip for 'of I. K.': Isambard Kingdom Brunel's giant steamship the Great Eastern was a commercial failure. 'Great' is part of the ship's name.
explanation.definitionFit: Brunel's vast iron steamship of 1858, the Great Eastern, lost money and ruined its backers.

clue.text: "Larkins comes tome" (H. G. Wells)
